q: In 1896, Henry Becquerel discovered that uranium salts emit radiations which affect photographic plates and cause ionization.
e: This is the exact historical discovery of radioactivity by Henry Becquerel.

q: The radiations are emitted from the nucleus of uranium atoms and are of four types; namely alpha, beta, gamma and delta rays.
e: The radiations emitted from the nucleus are of three types; namely alpha, beta and gamma rays.

q: The emission of some or all of alpha, beta and gamma rays from the nucleus of an unstable atom is called radioactivity.
e: This is the exact textbook definition of radioactivity.

q: Of all 92 elements which exist in nature, all heavy elements with atomic number greater than 83 are stable.
e: Only a few heavy elements with atomic number greater than 83 are radioactive or unstable, not stable.

q: Radium and polonium were discovered by Marie Curie.
e: Marie Curie discovered both radium and polonium among radioactive elements.

q: Radioactive elements can only be found in nature and cannot be artificially produced.
e: Radioactive elements can also be artificially produced using nuclear reactors and particle accelerators.

q: Alpha decay is a process in which an atomic nucleus emits an alpha particle and transforms into a different atomic nucleus, with mass number reduces by four and atomic number reduces by two.
e: This accurately describes the changes in mass and atomic numbers during alpha decay.

q: An alpha particle is a hydrogen nucleus.
e: An alpha particle is a helium nucleus, consisting of two protons and two neutrons.

q: Beta-minus decay is a process in which a neutron in an atomic nucleus changes to a proton with the emission of an electron and an antineutrino.
e: This is the exact mechanism of beta-minus decay.

q: In beta-minus decay, the mass number remains unchanged but atomic number decreases by one.
e: In beta-minus decay, the mass number remains unchanged but the atomic number increases by one.

q: Beta-plus decay is a process in which a proton in an atomic nucleus changes to a neutron with the emission of a positron and a neutrino.
e: This correctly defines the process of beta-plus decay.

q: The existence of positron was theoretically predicted by Anderson in 1931 and experimentally detected by Dirac in 1932.
e: The positron was theoretically predicted by Dirac in 1931 and experimentally detected by Anderson in 1932.

q: Positron, the antiparticle of electron, has the same mass and same magnitude of electric charge as an electron; but positron is positively charged.
e: This correctly describes the physical properties of a positron compared to an electron.

q: Neutrino, a fundamental particle as an electron, has a positive charge and a large rest mass.
e: A neutrino has no charge and a negligibly small rest mass.

q: For a nucleus to be stable, there must be an appropriate ratio of protons and neutrons.
e: Nuclear stability depends heavily on maintaining an appropriate proton-to-neutron ratio.

q: If a nucleus has excess protons, beta-minus decay takes place.
e: If a nucleus has excess neutrons, beta-minus decay takes place; a nucleus with excess protons undergoes beta-plus decay.

q: In gamma decay, the daughter nucleus resulting from alpha or beta decay is left in an excited state and it can then decay to a lower energy state by emitting a gamma ray photon.
e: This accurately describes the mechanism and cause of gamma decay.

q: In gamma decay, the atomic number and mass number of the parent and daughter nuclei change significantly.
e: In gamma decay, the atomic number and mass number of the parent and daughter nuclei remain unchanged.

q: Photons are massless and move at the speed of light in vacuum.
e: Photons are the quanta of the electromagnetic field and possess these exact properties.

q: The energy of a photon is directly proportional to the wavelength of the electromagnetic radiation associated with it.
e: The energy of a photon is inversely proportional to the wavelength of the electromagnetic radiation.

q: Alpha rays consist of helium nuclei, positively charged particles with a charge of +2e.
e: This correctly identifies the composition and charge of alpha particles.

q: Alpha rays cannot be deflected by electric and magnetic fields.
e: Because they are charged particles, alpha rays can be deflected by electric and magnetic fields.

q: Alpha rays are the most ionizing and the most penetrating of the three rays.
e: Alpha rays are the most ionizing but the least penetrating of the three rays.

q: Beta rays consist of either electrons or positrons moving with varying speeds.
e: Beta rays can be either beta-minus (electrons) or beta-plus (positrons).

q: Beta rays are more ionizing than alpha rays.
e: Beta rays are less ionizing than alpha rays.

q: Beta rays can be stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium.
e: This is the standard penetrating power limit for beta radiation.

q: Gamma rays are electromagnetic waves like light and X-rays, but have much longer wavelengths.
e: Gamma rays are electromagnetic waves but have much shorter wavelengths than light and X-rays.

q: Gamma rays have no charge and cannot be deflected by electric and magnetic fields.
e: Being uncharged electromagnetic waves, gamma rays are unaffected by electric and magnetic fields.

q: Gamma rays are the least ionizing and the least penetrating of the three rays.
e: Gamma rays are the least ionizing but the most penetrating of the three rays.

q: Intensity of gamma rays can be greatly reduced by several centimetres of lead but they are never completely stopped.
e: Lead significantly attenuates gamma rays, but theoretically they are never completely stopped.

q: The rate of decay of a radioactive sample is called activity.
e: Activity is defined as the rate at which alpha, beta particles or gamma rays are emitted.

q: SI unit for activity is curie (Ci).
e: The SI unit for activity is the becquerel (Bq); curie is an older, non-SI unit still in use.

q: 1 Ci is equal to $3.7 	imes 10^{10}$ event $s^{-1}$.
e: This is the exact numerical definition of one curie of activity.

q: The rate of decay is a characteristic of the radioactive element and it is strongly affected by the temperature.
e: The rate of decay is a characteristic of the radioactive element and it is unaffected by the temperature.

q: The half-life is defined as the time for half the atoms in a radioactive sample to decay.
e: This is the standard definition of radioactive half-life.

q: Radioactive decay is a deterministic process where it is possible to predict exactly when a particular atom will decay.
e: Radioactive decay is a statistical process; it is impossible to predict when a particular atom will decay.

q: A tracer is a small amount of radioactive isotope introduced into a system in order to follow the behaviour of some components of that system.
e: This is the exact definition of a radioactive tracer.

q: In medicine, radioactive iodine-131 is used as a tracer to check liver function.
e: Radioactive iodine-131 is used as a tracer to check thyroid function, not liver function.

q: In agriculture, radioisotope tracers like phosphorus-32 and nitrogen-15 are used to study the uptake of fertilizers.
e: These specific isotopes are used to study fertilizer uptake, retention, and utilization in plants.

q: Treatment with radiation is known as radiotherapy, and radioisotopes such as cobalt-60 and cesium-137 are widely used to treat cancer.
e: Cobalt-60 and cesium-137 are standard radioisotopes used in cancer radiotherapy.

q: In industrial gamma radiography, alpha emitters are used to inspect metal castings or welded joints.
e: In industrial gamma radiography, radioactive gamma emitters are used to inspect metal castings or welded joints.

q: The ability to use radioisotopes to accurately measure thickness is widely used as thickness monitoring system in the production of sheet materials.
e: Beta or gamma sources are routinely used in thickness monitors for materials like paper, plastics, and metal.

q: Carbon dating is a technique developed by Albert Einstein for estimating the age of the remains of plants and animals.
e: Carbon dating is a technique developed by Willard Libby, not Albert Einstein.

q: The half-life of carbon-14 is 5730 years.
e: This is the accepted half-life value for carbon-14 used in radioactive dating.

q: The abundance of carbon-14 in the atmosphere is essentially constant because it is continually produced by cosmic rays entering the upper atmosphere.
e: Cosmic ray neutrons bombard nitrogen-14 to continually replenish atmospheric carbon-14.

q: When an animal or a plant dies, the carbon cycle stops and the carbon-14 in the remain gradually increases by radioactive decay.
e: When an organism dies, the carbon-14 in the remain gradually decreases by radioactive decay.

q: The age of igneous rocks can be estimated from the proportion of potassium-40 to argon-40.
e: Potassium-40 decays into stable argon-40, allowing for the radioactive dating of rocks.

q: Gamma and neutron irradiation of seeds can be used to induce mutations to develop desired mutants that are resistant to disease.
e: Irradiation induces beneficial agricultural mutations for higher yields and disease resistance.

q: Irradiation of food increases the microbes in food and promotes insect infestation.
e: Irradiation of food is used to destroy microbes and control insect and parasite infestation.
